blocks.title: Is a number always smaller than its own square?
body: Square 6 and you get 36. Square −6 and you get 36 as well — the minus sign disappears, and both numbers land at the same height on the curve $y=x^2$. Now try one half. Now try 1. Does squaring really push every number further out?
blocks.footer: Test three numbers before you decide — one large, one between 0 and 1, one negative.

blocks.title: Three side lengths build one triangle, and only one
body: So once you have matched all three sides of one triangle to the three sides of another, you are finished measuring. Every angle already agrees.
It does not claim the two triangles sit the same way up — one may be turned or flipped over. Same shape and size, not the same position.

blocks.title: Find every point on $y=x^2$ at a height of 9
body: On this curve the height of a point is its $y$ value, and every point has coordinates $(x,x^2)$.
steps: Set the height equal to 9, which gives the equation $x^2=9$.
Solve it: $x=3$ or $x=-3$, because $-3$ times $-3$ is also 9.
Those two values are the same distance either side of the $y$-axis, so the curve reaches height 9 twice.
The curve therefore passes through $(3,9)$ and $(-3,9)$.
blocks.footer: Check each answer by substituting back.

blocks.title: How would you convince someone that the parabola is symmetric?
body: Look back at your table of values for $y=x^2$. Pick a pair of points the same distance either side of the $y$-axis, say what their coordinates have in common, and explain why that makes the two halves of the curve congruent.
blocks.footer: Answer in a full sentence that gives a reason — a number on its own is not an explanation.

blocks.title: Triangle ABC, built from three sides
blocks.caption: Each side length is fixed; the angles follow from them.

companion.title: Three sides are enough to fix a triangle
body: Nobody chose the angles here. They were settled the moment the three lengths were. Read the three measures marked at $A$, $B$ and $C$: each one is a consequence, not a decision.
companion.footer: Build it yourself with ruler and compasses, then check your angles against these.

blocks.title: The curve y = x²
blocks.caption: Two points are marked: the vertex V and the point P at (2, 4).

companion.title: Reading a rule off the curve
body: Begin at $V$, the turning point at the bottom of the curve. Fold the page down the vertical axis and the two arms land on each other.
Now follow the right arm out to $P$. Read its coordinates off the grid, square the $x$ you read, and see whether $y=x^2$ gives back the height.
companion.footer: Where does P's mirror sit on the left arm?
